gaps.text: Combining several spectroscopy methods (data fusion) (Low-level fusion: UV-Vis (or its ATR variant) and Raman spectra from the same sampling spot are synchronised to a common time step and merged into one augmented matrix, with block scaling so neither method dominates. Each method keeps its own calibration and diagnostics, since a fused model breaks when any block drifts. The fused model must beat the best single method on held-out runs, otherwise the extra instrument is dropped.)
Yeast-fermentation-specific performance figures (accuracy, detection limits, response times) for any of the shortlisted methods
Achievable in-line fiber length for the selected configuration at the customer's installation distance
One optical measurement can serve both the biomass and the metabolic signal.

items.finding: Low-level data fusion is described as the simplest combination approach, where variables from different sources are concatenated into a single new data matrix.
items.how_it_applies: This supports the planned augmented-matrix design for O3; the feasibility study should implement the concatenation as described and verify the fused model against the best single method on held-out runs before committing to the second instrument.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: The review is general PAT literature, not yeast fermentation or UV-Vis/Raman fusion specifically, and it does not state that fusion improves performance in any given case.

citation.quote: Low-level data fusion (LLDF) is considered the simplest method to achieve a combination of inputs. In this case, the data is rearranged into a new data matrix, where the variables coming from different sources are placed one after the other.
citation.label: E02 ¶31

items.finding: The review states that the contribution and complementarity of each dataset must be evaluated before fusing data from multiple sources.
items.how_it_applies: This justifies building single-method calibrations with their own diagnostics first, then testing whether the fused model actually beats the best single method; if not, the extra instrument can be dropped.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: It is a methodological recommendation from a general review, not a demonstrated result for this broth, matrix or instrument pair.

citation.quote: Before fusing data from multiple sources, it is essential to evaluate the contribution of each dataset to the model and its complementarity.
citation.label: E02 ¶82

items.finding: A cited Raman and FT-IR food study showed that instrument complementarity alone did not always improve prediction of several quality attributes.
items.how_it_applies: This is a concrete reason to include a drop-the-second-instrument criterion in the feasibility design rather than assuming O3 outperforms O2.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: The example is a food application with Raman/FT-IR, not UV-Vis/Raman in fermenting broth, so the outcome may differ here.

citation.quote: In some situations, instrument complementarity (not data complementarity) was not sufficient to improve the performance of predictive several CQAs, as shown by a Raman and FT-IR data based food analytical study [73].
citation.label: E02 ¶36

items.finding: Raman spectroscopy is frequently used in upstream processing because of its high selectivity and low water interference, but with relatively long measurement times.
items.how_it_applies: This supports Raman (O2) as a candidate for optically dense aqueous broth, while flagging measurement time as a parameter to quantify in the feasibility study against the customer's need for early change detection.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: The statement is a general review remark without performance figures for yeast fermentation, and measurement times depend on the specific instrument and probe configuration.

citation.quote: Raman spectroscopy is frequently applied in upstream processing in research and industry due to its high selectivity and low water interference [55] despite the relatively long measurement times.
citation.label: E01 ¶20
